title: Stars: Birth and Main Sequence
welcome_lead: From cold nebula to nuclear furnace — the protostar story.
meta_desc: A-Level Astronomy: protostars, hydrostatic equilibrium and main sequence.
final_note: A main-sequence star is a long, stable balance between gravity and pressure.

walkthroughs.body_html: Stars form in cold molecular clouds. Gravity collapses denser regions; falling gas heats up and forms a protostar. When the core reaches about 10 million K, hydrogen fusion begins.
On the main sequence, gravity pulling inward is exactly balanced by gas and radiation pressure pushing outward. This hydrostatic equilibrium keeps stars stable for millions to billions of years.
Low-mass stars use the proton-proton chain; higher-mass stars use the CNO cycle. Both net 4 hydrogen nuclei into 1 helium, releasing energy via mass-energy equivalence E = mc^2.

It is the largest stage of a star's life.
Whether it has planets.

mcqs.q: What determines whether a star becomes a white dwarf or a neutron star?
options: Because they are the brightest objects in the universe.
Its mass - low/medium mass becomes a white dwarf; massive stars produce neutron stars or black holes.
Its colour during its main sequence phase.
Whether it has planets.

They have nearly uniform peak brightness, so their apparent brightness reveals distance.
Whether it has planets.
Because they are the brightest objects in the universe.
